title: Nouns and Noun Structures
orientation: Nouns do more than name objects. They let you present an idea as a separate item, a substance, a group or a process, and those choices affect articles, quantity expressions and agreement. Today develops the noun framework introduced on Day 1. You will practise regular and irregular plurals, learn how countability depends on a word’s sense, and build noun phrases that identify their meaning precisely. You will also distinguish ordinary plurals from genitives and use nominalisation without losing information about who acted. Everyday inventories, academic descriptions and formal reports all depend on these choices. Begin with short phrases before analysing longer ones. The advanced material explains why legitimate forms such as two coffees, the committee are and a friend of mine should not be corrected by applying an exceptionless slogan.
outcomes: Form the taught regular, irregular and compound plurals.
Choose count-unit expressions for ordinary noncount nouns.
Explain a contextual countability change and a British collective-agreement choice.
Write singular, plural and double-genitive constructions accurately.
Analyse noun modifiers, apposition and a meaning-preserving nominalisation.

modules.title: Noun meanings and the formation of plurals
modules.definition: A noun is a word class whose members typically head noun phrases. Meaning labels such as concrete, abstract, collective and material describe overlapping kinds of nouns; number is the grammatical contrast between singular and plural where that contrast is available.
foundation: A common noun identifies a kind: river, student or proposal. A proper noun is conventionally a name: Aisha, Lahore or the Indus. Concrete nouns refer to things ordinarily perceived through the senses, such as a bell; abstract nouns refer to qualities, states or ideas, such as fairness. A collective noun names a group, such as committee. A material noun names a substance, such as copper. These labels overlap: committee is common and collective, while copper is common, concrete and material in its substance meaning. They are not seven exclusive boxes into which every noun must fit.
intermediate: Regular count plurals normally add -s or -es: roads, boxes, wishes. Consonant plus y usually changes to -ies, as city/cities; vowel plus y normally keeps y, as key/keys. Plural forms must be learned with the noun when spelling is irregular: child/children, woman/women, mouse/mice, tooth/teeth. Some nouns keep one form for both numbers: one sheep, six sheep. Check the whole expression before choosing a verb, since the spelling alone may not reveal number. Apostrophes do not form ordinary plurals: three shops, not three shop’s.
advanced: Some borrowed nouns retain foreign-origin patterns: analysis/analyses, criterion/criteria and phenomenon/phenomena. Others have established alternatives: indexes and indices or appendixes and appendices. Meaning and field can affect which plural is conventional; consult a current dictionary or disciplinary style guide rather than assume the older-looking form is always superior. Compound plurals usually mark the noun that functions as head: two car parks and three sisters-in-law. In lexicalised compounds the exact form can be conventional, so memorising the complete singular/plural pair is safer than applying a spelling slogan to every multiword expression.
expert: Proper names can acquire count uses without losing their connection to naming. Two Aishas may mean two people called Aisha; a Picasso may mean a work by Picasso. This is a contextual shift, not evidence that proper nouns never take articles or plurals. Semantic categories also shift with sense: glass is a substance in broken glass and a count object in three glasses. Number, countability and reference interact but are distinct. A grammatically plural word is not necessarily a group noun, and a collective singular does not necessarily denote just one person. Analyse the particular lexical sense and noun phrase.

patterns.meaning: Usually add -s/-es, but retain the noun’s established irregular form.

patterns.form: head noun inside a compound → plural head
patterns.meaning: sister-in-law → sisters-in-law; car park → car parks.

examples.analysis: Children is an irregular plural; trees is a regular plural.
Analyses is the plural of analysis; it is distinct from the verb analyses.
The plural marks sisters, the head of this compound.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first requests a material; the second requests countable objects or containers.

exceptions: A noun’s spelling may remain unchanged: this sheep is restless but these sheep are restless. The determiner and verb make number explicit.

mistakes.reason: The established plural of criterion is criteria.
A consonant before final y normally produces the plural spelling -ies.

glossary.definition: A noun naming a group as a group.
The singular/plural distinction expressed in relevant forms and agreement.

modules.title: Countability, special number patterns and group agreement
modules.definition: Countability describes how a noun sense combines with numbers and determiners. A count use presents separate units; a noncount use presents a mass, substance, activity or abstraction without ordinary unit counting. The distinction is grammatical and depends on lexical meaning and context.
foundation: Count nouns permit expressions such as a chair and several chairs. Noncount nouns in ordinary senses combine with some or much rather than a/an and do not take ordinary plural -s: information, advice, furniture, equipment, evidence and research. Use a piece of information, two items of equipment, three chairs or several studies when units matter. Evidence is not counted as evidences in ordinary general prose; a piece of evidence or several kinds of evidence states the intended unit. Learn each noun in a complete phrase, especially where another language uses a different countability pattern.
intermediate: A noun may have count and noncount senses. Experience means accumulated knowledge in She has experience, but an experience names a particular event. Two coffees can mean two servings; different wines can mean types. These changes are conventional, not permission to count every noncount noun freely. Advice and information normally retain their noncount pattern in everyday and academic prose. Much research is natural formal English. Where specialised dictionaries document a restricted plural, such as researches for particular investigations, identify that sense and register; use studies or research projects as the transparent general default.
advanced: Some nouns have special number patterns. News and mathematics take singular agreement in their ordinary topic meanings despite final -s. Scissors, trousers, goods and belongings normally have plural form and agreement. One pair of scissors is singular because pair heads the expression; two pairs of scissors are plural. People is normally plural when meaning persons, while peoples can refer to distinct populations. Police normally takes a plural verb when referring to officers collectively. A noun’s final letters do not therefore predict either its countability or the verb automatically. Check its meaning and its head phrase.
expert: British group nouns can take singular agreement for a unit or plural agreement for members: The team is ready; The team are changing into their different uniforms. American English generally prefers singular agreement with a formally singular collective; the members of the team makes a plural construal explicit in either variety. Avoid claiming that a country has one exceptionless rule for all collectives. Keep the intended perspective clear when choosing pronouns. A group’s membership can be many people even when its grammar is singular; grammatical number and real-world number are different kinds of information. Day 10 develops these agreement choices further.

patterns.meaning: A countable unit expression allows explicit counting without inventing a plural of the material noun.

examples.sentence: The technician replaced two items of equipment.
examples.analysis: Items supplies countable units; equipment retains its ordinary noncount form.

examples.sentence: The news is encouraging, but the police are cautious.
examples.analysis: News is grammatically singular; police normally requires plural agreement.

examples.sentence: The committee are exchanging their separate notes.
examples.analysis: A British member-focused plural is appropriate; the members of the committee is a clear alternative.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first concerns knowledge; the second concerns separate events.

exceptions: A countability shift needs an established interpretation: two teas readily means servings, but two advices is not the ordinary way to request two recommendations.

mistakes.repair: We received three useful pieces of information.
mistakes.reason: Count pieces, not information, in this ordinary informational sense.

mistakes.problem: The new trousers is too long.
mistakes.repair: The new trousers are too long.
mistakes.reason: Trousers is plural in this use. A new pair of trousers would instead have singular pair as its head and take is.

glossary.definition: A noun use not ordinarily counted by a/an or a numeral directly.
Agreement influenced by the meaning or construal of the subject.
glossary.example: The team are sharing their opinions presents individual members.

modules.title: Genitives, possession and noun relationships
modules.definition: The genitive is a construction commonly marked by -’s or an apostrophe in writing. It expresses several relationships, including possession, association, authorship and time. An of-construction is another way to relate noun phrases, but the two patterns are not always interchangeable.
foundation: With an ordinary singular noun, write the student’s notebook. With a regular plural ending in s, write the students’ notebooks. With an irregular plural, write the children’s notebooks. First determine how many owners or associates are meant, then place the apostrophe. The apostrophe is not a general signal that a word ends in s. Compare two teachers, one teacher’s desk and two teachers’ desks: the three expressions communicate different grammatical information. Possessive pronouns such as hers, ours and theirs do not take an additional apostrophe.
intermediate: The genitive often acts like a determiner: Amina’s bicycle identifies a bicycle through its relation to Amina. The relationship is not always literal ownership. Amina’s article may mean the article she wrote; tomorrow’s meeting relates the event to a time; the committee’s decision identifies its institutional source. The report’s conclusion and the conclusion of the report are both normal. People and organisations often favour the -’s pattern, while long phrases or some part–whole relationships may favour of. These are usage tendencies, not a grammatical rule that inanimate nouns can never take -’s.
advanced: Place the marker at the end of a relevant compound or phrase: my sister-in-law’s address. In a shared genitive, Sara and Imran’s proposal can identify one joint proposal; Sara’s and Imran’s separate proposals makes separate association explicit. The exact punctuation and wording can become awkward with pronouns or long coordination, so recast rather than rely on punctuation to carry an unclear meaning. Names ending in s allow editorial alternatives such as James’s and James’; follow a consistent style and recognise both. Do not mark one conventional style as universally ungrammatical.
expert: A double-genitive construction combines of with a genitive: a friend of Amina’s or a colleague of mine. It can select one member of an associated set and differs from of + object pronoun. A portrait of Amina depicts Amina; a portrait of Amina’s associates the portrait with her, often as owner or creator, depending on context. The marker’s ability to occur at a phrase edge motivates analysing it as a clitic in many modern grammars; traditional teaching often calls it a possessive ending. Knowing both labels is useful, but the practical task remains deciding the intended relationship and the exact phrase the marker belongs to.

patterns.meaning: the visitor’s coat; the visitors’ coats
a neighbour of mine; a friend of Leena’s

examples.sentence: The doctor’s bag was beside the doctors’ coats.
examples.analysis: The first genitive is singular; the second is regular plural.

examples.sentence: The company’s response arrived after a week’s delay.
examples.analysis: The genitives express an institutional source and a duration.

examples.sentence: A colleague of my brother’s has rented the flat.
examples.analysis: The outer expression selects a colleague through the genitive phrase my brother’s.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical; depiction is the usual first reading, while the second associates ownership or authorship with Nida.

exceptions: Names ending in s have style-dependent written genitives. James’s answer and James’ answer should not be used as competing right/wrong choices without a specified editorial convention.

mistakes.reason: Children is an irregular plural without final plural -s, so the marker is ’s.
The possessive pronoun hers has no apostrophe.

glossary.definition: A grammatical construction marking a relation between noun phrases.
glossary.example: The researcher’s notes identify notes through the researcher.

glossary.definition: An of-construction followed by a genitive expression.

modules.title: Noun phrases, modifiers, apposition and nominalisation
modules.definition: A noun phrase is organised around a noun or pronoun head and may contain determiners, modifiers and complements. Nominalisation forms or uses a noun to express an event, process or quality. Apposition places related noun phrases together to identify or describe a referent.
foundation: Expand a simple noun step by step: report; the report; the detailed report; the detailed report on housing. Report remains the head. The specifies reference, detailed modifies it before the head and on housing adds information after the head. These dependents belong inside the same noun phrase. When the phrase acts as subject, recognise the whole unit rather than report alone. Expansion helps a writer be precise, but putting every available detail before a head makes a phrase difficult to read. Place information where its relationship is clearest.
intermediate: Nouns can function as premodifiers: a research centre, a school library and an application form. The first noun does not become an adjective merely because it modifies another noun. A noun–noun expression can name many relationships: a school bus serves a school, a stone wall is made of stone and a history teacher teaches history. The relation must be learned from meaning and convention. Noun modifiers are often singular, but established plural modifiers occur in a sports centre and a savings account. Do not mechanically delete every -s before a second noun.
advanced: Apposition offers another way to identify: my colleague Farah integrates the name into the phrase, while Farah, our new coordinator, adds a supplementary description. Punctuation depends on whether information identifies or supplements, so do not add commas merely because a second noun phrase appears. Noun phrases can also contain complements such as the decision to postpone the inspection, where the infinitival clause specifies the decision’s content. Longer phrases may embed other phrases: applications from graduates of local colleges. Their hierarchical structure matters more than a flat list of nearby words.
expert: Nominalisation allows an action or quality to become a noun: the council approved the plan becomes the council’s approval of the plan; the road is wide relates to the width of the road. This can make an event a topic that later sentences discuss. It can also hide who acted: the approval alone leaves the decision-maker unstated. Preserve agency, time and modality when rewriting. The proposal for a new inspection system is different from the proposal’s inspection system: the former identifies proposed content, while the latter may assign a system to a proposal awkwardly. Choose a structure for the relationship you intend, not merely because it sounds formal.

patterns.meaning: The two recent reports on flooding are one expanded noun phrase.
The council approved the plan → the council’s approval of the plan.

examples.sentence: The research centre needs a new application form.
examples.analysis: Research and application are noun modifiers, not necessarily adjectives.

examples.sentence: Our neighbour, a retired engineer, repaired the pump.
examples.analysis: The supplementary appositive describes the already identified neighbour.

examples.sentence: The committee’s rejection of the revised timetable surprised the applicants.
examples.analysis: Rejection nominalises reject; the genitive preserves the rejecting body and of preserves the rejected content.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The event is a verb predicate in the first and a noun-phrase topic in the second.

exceptions: Plural modifiers may be conventional: a sports centre is standard. Dictionary-backed established compounds override a beginner’s singular-modifier tendency.

mistakes.problem: The libraries research needs more funding. Intended: research carried out by the library.
mistakes.repair: The library’s research needs more funding.
mistakes.reason: The intended source relation is expressed by a genitive, not an unexplained plural modifier.

mistakes.problem: The council’s approved of the plan was unexpected.
mistakes.repair: The council’s approval of the plan was unexpected.
mistakes.reason: The genitive requires a noun head here; approval is the relevant nominalisation.

glossary.definition: A construction placing noun phrases together with a shared identifying or descriptive relationship.
Use or formation of a noun to express an event, process or quality.

questions.prompt: Which is the established plural of criterion?
questions.why: Criteria is the established ordinary plural. Criterion is singular, criterias adds an inappropriate plural ending, and criterion’s is a genitive form rather than an ordinary plural.

questions.prompt: For ordinary general prose, choose the completed phrase: two useful ____ about the deadline.
questions.why: Information is noncount in this sense; pieces supplies countable units. The other choices misuse number or invent a form.

questions.prompt: Several children share one reading room. Which genitive is correct?
questions.why: Children is an irregular plural, so the genitive adds ’s; no extra plural -s or second apostrophe is needed.

questions.prompt: In the phrase the new school library, which word is the noun head?
questions.why: Library is the head; the is a determiner, new an adjective and school a noun modifier.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately describes two coffees at a café?
options: Every noncount noun can therefore take two directly.
The numeral turns coffees into a verb.
Coffees is a conventional count use meaning servings.
Coffee can never have a count use.
questions.why: Servings license this count use, but such shifts depend on the noun and context.

questions.prompt: Choose agreement with singular head pair: This pair of scissors ____ new.
questions.why: Pair is the singular head. Scissors alone normally has plural agreement, but does not control this verb.

questions.prompt: Check the labels: The visitors’ coats [A] / were hanging [B] / beside the door [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
questions.why: The regular plural visitors forms its genitive with an apostrophe after s; plural coats agrees with were.

questions.prompt: Check ordinary informational prose: The adviser offered [A] / several practical advices [B] / before the meeting [C]. Choose the faulty part or No error.
questions.why: Advice is noncount in this sense. Several pieces of practical advice repairs the phrase; the other parts are well formed.

questions.prompt: Which plural correctly marks the head of sister-in-law?
questions.why: Sisters is the head plural in the established compound; law and in do not receive the plural marker.

questions.prompt: Which account of British The team are sharing their separate views is accurate?
options: Plural agreement presents the members individually.
It is ungrammatical in every variety.
Team is always a plural-form noun.
Their proves that team cannot ever take is.
questions.why: British collective agreement can reflect members; singular unit construal is also possible in other contexts.

questions.prompt: Classify copper as used in Copper conducts heat using common/proper and concrete/abstract/material labels.
questions.model: Copper is a common noun; in this use it is concrete and material.
rubric: Allow overlapping semantic labels.
Do not call a material noun a separate exclusive word class.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Complete these established number pairs: one child / three ____; one analysis / two ____.
rubric: Use the irregular plural children.
Distinguish noun analyses from singular analysis.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain the countability difference: Her experience is valuable; Her experiences abroad changed her plans.
questions.model: Experience means accumulated knowledge in the first and separate events in the second.
rubric: Connect countability to meaning.
Explain why plural is legitimate in the second use.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Request three separate units of equipment without pluralising equipment.
questions.model: We need three items of equipment.
rubric: Provide a countable unit head.
Keep equipment in its noncount form.
alternatives: Three pieces of equipment is also acceptable.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the notebooks belonging to several teachers using a genitive.
rubric: Mark teachers as plural.
Place the apostrophe after the plural s.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Mark the whole noun phrase and its head in The two recent reports on water use were helpful.
questions.model: Whole subject noun phrase: The two recent reports on water use. Head: reports.
rubric: Include the postmodifier on water use.
Distinguish the head from the full subject.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain two possible relationships in noun compounds by analysing a stone wall and a history teacher.
questions.model: A stone wall is made of stone; a history teacher teaches history.
rubric: Keep both first words as nouns in these uses.
Name the different semantic relationships.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Compare The committee is ready with The committee are comparing their private notes in British English.
questions.model: Singular presents the committee as a unit; plural presents members and their individual actions.
rubric: Recognise both as available British patterns.
Relate the pronoun choice to the stated perspective.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain why a photograph of Imran and a photograph of Imran’s can differ.
questions.model: The first normally depicts Imran; the second associates the photograph with Imran, often as owner or creator.
rubric: Explain depiction versus association.
Acknowledge context for ownership or authorship.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Add the supplied description as a supplementary appositive: Amina welcomed the visitors. Amina is the project coordinator.
questions.model: Amina, the project coordinator, welcomed the visitors.
rubric: Use paired commas for the supplementary phrase.
Preserve the identity and welcoming event.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Nominalise approved while keeping who acted and what was approved: The panel approved the revised plan. Start with The panel’s.
questions.model: The panel’s approval of the revised plan
rubric: Use approval as noun head.
Retain panel as the approving body and revised plan as content.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Why can Two Leenas work in this office be grammatical even though Leena is a proper name?
questions.model: The count use means two people called Leena. A name can acquire a conventional contextual count interpretation.
rubric: Give the name-based reading.
Do not infer that proper names always lack plural forms.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Identify the grammatical number of news, trousers and mathematics in their ordinary general senses.
questions.model: News: singular; trousers: plural; mathematics as an academic subject: singular.
rubric: Treat final -s as an unreliable number test.
State the ordinary senses being analysed.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain the genitive relationships in yesterday’s announcement and the architect’s design.
questions.model: Yesterday’s relates announcement to time; architect’s may identify the creator of the design. Neither is limited to literal ownership.
rubric: Name time and authorship.
Avoid defining every genitive as ownership.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Arrange into a noun phrase referring to a form used for applications: new / application / the / form.
rubric: Use form as head.
Keep application as a noun modifier and new as an adjective.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Repair ordinary countability and number errors: The equipments is expensive. The news are worrying. We need two furnitures.
questions.model: The equipment is expensive. The news is worrying. We need two items of furniture.
rubric: Keep equipment and furniture noncount.
Give singular agreement to news.
Use a count unit for two items.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Analyse applications from graduates of local colleges as nested units.
questions.model: Applications is the outer head; from graduates of local colleges modifies it. Graduates heads the phrase inside from; of local colleges modifies graduates.
rubric: Identify applications as outer head.
Show that of local colleges belongs with graduates rather than directly with applications.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: A scientist chooses indices for a mathematical context while a librarian writes indexes. Why should a learner check sense and field rather than declare one plural wrong?
questions.model: Both plural forms are established; conventions can differ by sense and field. A dictionary and local disciplinary style guide determine the appropriate choice.
rubric: Recognise both as established.
Connect choice to context rather than assumed historical superiority.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct ordinary general prose: The office bought new furnitures.
rubric: Remove the inappropriate plural ending.
Keep the purchase meaning.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

rubric: Use plural agreement with scissors.
Retain these.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct: The report contains three analysises.
rubric: Use the established plural analyses.
Keep three separate analyses.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Several students own these files. Correct: The student’s files were collected.
rubric: Use plural students from the stated context.
Place the apostrophe after plural s.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct the nominalisation: The board’s reject of the offer was unexpected.
corrections.model: The board’s rejection of the offer was unexpected.
rubric: Use rejection as the noun head.
Preserve the board and offer relationships.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct ordinary advice-giving prose: She gave us many useful advices.
corrections.model: She gave us much useful advice.
rubric: Use noncount advice.
Replace many with a compatible quantifier or unit expression.
alternatives: She gave us several useful pieces of advice.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if necessary in British English: The staff are sharing their opinions.
rubric: Recognise a British member-focused collective reading.
Do not impose singular agreement as universal.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if necessary: The new sports centre opens on Monday.
rubric: Recognise the established plural noun modifier sports.
Do not mechanically change it to sport.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

transformations.prompt: Express one shared proposal by Nadia and Bilal with a joint genitive, then give an unambiguous of-paraphrase.
transformations.model: Nadia and Bilal’s joint proposal; the joint proposal of Nadia and Bilal.
rubric: Make shared ownership explicit.
Preserve both names and singular proposal.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

transformations.prompt: Turn The inspector’s examination of the roof took an hour into a clause using examined; keep agent, object and duration.
transformations.model: The inspector examined the roof for an hour.
rubric: Recover inspector as agent and roof as object.
Preserve the one-hour duration.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

writing.prompt: Write 80–110 words describing a small school, office or workshop inventory. Use three count nouns, three noncount nouns, one genitive and one expanded noun phrase. Identify those forms afterwards.
writing.model:
The workshop has four benches and several cupboards. Its equipment is old but reliable, and the technicians inspect it before each class. Two assistants keep a list of spare parts beside the entrance. The supervisor’s notebook contains information about repairs and advice for new staff. A pair of protective glasses hangs near each bench, where it can be reached easily. The recent report on safety recommends better lighting in the storage area. Until that work is finished, the team keeps the passage clear and asks visitors to use the main entrance.

Analysis: Benches, cupboards and assistants are count nouns. Equipment, information and advice are noncount here. The supervisor’s is a genitive; the recent report on safety is an expanded noun phrase.
rubric: Use each required noun pattern in a meaningful context.
Keep noncount nouns and plural-only nouns compatible with their determiners and verbs.
Identify actual examples from the writing rather than merely list terms.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 1: identify the subject head and whole subject in The new safety equipment arrived.
recall.model: Head: equipment. Whole subject: The new safety equipment.
rubric: Identify the complete noun phrase.
Do not make safety an adjective merely because it modifies equipment.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 1: distinguish the derivational and inflectional endings in painters.
recall.model: Paint + -er forms a person noun; -s marks plural.
rubric: Name the two different processes.
Identify painter as the stem receiving plural marking.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 1: in The cupboard is empty, identify empty’s class and function.
recall.model: Empty is an adjective functioning as subject complement.
rubric: Give both class and function.
Do not label empty a direct object.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

checklist: I check a noun’s sense before deciding countability.
I distinguish ordinary plural endings from genitive markers.
I can explain a group-as-unit and group-as-members reading.
I identify the head inside a long noun phrase.
I preserve the actor and affected entity when nominalising a clause.
